entries.note: Pokorny IEW 55-61 heads the article '1. ar-, themat. (a)rē-, schwere Basis arə-, rē- und i-Basis (ə)rī-, rei- ... "fügen, passen"'; Watkins/AHD prints 'ar-. Also arə-. To fit together. [Pok. 1. ar- 55.]' — Nourai's root name, language label, gloss and page reference are copied from AHD and are correct. In current laryngealist notation the root is *h₂er-. Two cross-cutting caveats: (a) most of Nourai's Latin/Greek/Germanic material is lifted verbatim from the 1975 AHD appendix (the gloss 'ôrdô: row of threads in loom' is Watkins' own wording), and where Watkins hedges ('Possibly suffixed variant form (or separate root) *ōr-dh-'; 'Variant or separate root *rē-') Nourai drops the hedge — the *rē-dh- branch that carries Old Persian rādiy, Persian rā and English read is reconstructed by most current handbooks as an independent root *Hreh₁dʰ-, and Pokorny himself calls the link of Latin ōrdō to ar- 'ganz fraglich' (IEW 61). (b) The whole Greek→Arabic→Persian branch (harma → 'araba → ارابه) is rejected by every reference consulted: Lokotsch files araba as Turkish, Wiktionary as Turkic of uncertain ultimate origin, Asbaghi as a Persian word arabicised, and Borhan-e Qate' gives no etymology at all.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *h₂er- (در نگارش قدیم‌تر *ar-/*arə-) به معنی «جور کردن، به هم پیوستن، سامان دادن» است؛ پوکورنی آن را در فرهنگ ریشه‌شناسی هندوژرمنی، صفحات ۵۵ تا ۶۱، با معنی «fügen, passen» آورده و واتکینز در پیوست فرهنگ American Heritage عیناً «to fit together» را با ارجاع به «Pok. 1. ar- 55» ثبت کرده است؛ پس نام ریشه، برچسب زبانی و معنی در نمودار نورایی درست است. دو نکتهٔ کلی: نخست آنکه شاخهٔ *rē-dh- (که پارسی باستان rādiy و «را»ی فارسی و read انگلیسی از آن می‌آید) در پژوهش امروزی غالباً ریشه‌ای جداگانه (*Hreh₁dʰ-) شمرده می‌شود و حتی خود پوکورنی پیوند ōrdō لاتینی را با این ریشه «کاملاً مشکوک» می‌خواند؛ دوم آنکه شاخهٔ یونانی ← عربی ← فارسی (harma ← عربة ← ارابه) را هیچ‌یک از مآخذ تأیید نمی‌کند و لوکوچ، ویکی‌واژه و اصباغی آن را واژه‌ای ترکی (یا فارسی معرَّب) می‌دانند نه یونانی.

nodes.derivation: Avestan ratu- m. is the thematic t-stem *r̥-tu- built to the zero grade of *h₂er- ('that which is set right / put in order'), the exact formal counterpart of Vedic r̥tú- 'fixed time, order, rule' and of Latin artus, -ūs 'joint'. In the Gathas it is 'judge, arbiter, one who pronounces the ratu (judgement)'; in the Younger Avesta it is the 'Ratu', the model or patron of each class of beings and, in the liturgy, the priestly office paired with the ahu- (ahu-ca ratu-ca 'overlord and chief judge'). Bartholomae AiW cols. 1498-1500 gives ¹ratav- 'Richter, Meister' and ³ratav- 'Judicium, Richterspruch'; Pokorny 56 quotes it as 'ratu- m. "Richter, Schiedsrichter" und "Zeitraum" (gemeinsame Grundbedeutung etwa "Zurechtlegung", woraus "Zurechtlegung des Rechts" und "richtiger Zeitpunkt")'. Nourai's gloss 'judge, religious leader' covers both the Gathic and the Younger-Avestan usage and is accurate.

nodes.derivation: Avestan ratu- > Middle Persian rad by the two regular Middle Iranian changes: intervocalic/post-vocalic -t- is voiced to -d- (Av. pitar- > MP pidar, Av. ratu- > MP rad) and the final -u of the u-stem is lost with the collapse of Old Iranian nominal inflection. MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary p. 70 gives 'rad [ltl] (spiritual) chief, master. ~īh: office of rad' and, on the same page, the derivative 'radunay [/twny = Av. ratunaya-] one under the guidance of a rad', which makes the Avestan source explicit. Nyberg's glossary s.v. rat spells the Book Pahlavi ⟨lt'⟩ and glosses it '"genius", divinity or tutelary spirit presiding over one of the categories ... into which all beings of the good creation are divided ... Av. ²ratu-; NP rad'. The word is a technical term of the Zoroastrian priesthood (Pahlavi rad = the dastwar), which is why Nourai's 'leader, master, Sir' is right for the Middle Persian stage.

nodes.derivation: New Persian رَد rad continues Middle Persian rad unchanged (no further sound change is involved; the word survives mainly as an archaism of the Zoroastrian and epic register). Nushin's Vāzhe-nāmak, the Shahnameh glossary, states the chain outright: 'رد (با زبر اول) از ریشهٔ اوستایی رتو ratu، پهلوی رت rat، به معنی بزرگ و سرور مینوی (پورداود، ویسپرد ص ۹۱). در گات‌ها به معنی داور (پورداود، یادداشت‌های گات‌ها ۱۲). "دانا و بخرد" (لغت فرس، صحاح)', and it quotes exactly the Ferdowsi line Nourai reproduces ('دل بخردان داشت و مغز ردان'). Borhan-e Qate' glosses رد 'حکیم و دانشمند - و خواجه - و پهلوان و دلاور و بهادر', which matches Nourai's 'leader, judge, hero, wise' term for term. Wiktionary's Persian رد (etymology 1) has '(archaic) sage (wise person); an important person in Zoroastrianism'. The only complication is that Horn (no. 601) files Pahlavi rat (as a title) under رَاد rād 'generous' (Av. rāiti-, Skt. rāti-); Bartholomae, MacKenzie and Nyberg keep the two apart, and Nushin's Avestan derivation is the one modern scholarship follows.

nodes.derivation: Both forms are real and both stand on Pokorny's p. 56, but the labels are not quite right. (a) Av. arəṇte (Nourai's 'arânte') is the 3rd plural present middle of ar- and Pokorny glosses it 'sie setzen sich fest, bleiben stecken' — 'they set themselves firmly, stay put', i.e. the intransitive/middle 'fit oneself in place', not the transitive 'puts in order' of the chart; it is the Iranian counterpart of Greek ἀραρίσκω 'I fit together' and of Skt. r̥ṇóti/r̥ccháti. (b) 'arem' is Avestan arəm, an adverb 'passend, entsprechend' ('fittingly, properly', e.g. in arəm-piθwā 'meal-time, the time fitting for a meal'), from the zero grade with the adverbial ending -əm; but 'aram' with plain -a- is the Sanskrit twin áram/álam 'fittingly, enough' (whence álaṃ-kar- 'to adorn'), which Pokorny lists in the same breath — Nourai has silently put a Vedic form in an Avestan box. The derivation from *h₂er- is not in doubt for either word; only the gloss of arəṇte and the language label of aram are loose.

nodes.derivation: Old Persian rādiy (𐎼𐎠𐎭𐎡𐎹) is the locative singular of a stem rād- 'reason, cause', used as a postposition governing the genitive, 'on account of, for the sake of'. Kent's Lexicon (Old Persian, p. 205) reads: 'rādiy ... various uses, often affixed to direct object for clarity; also OCS radi, postpos. with gen., "on account of"; loc. sg. of rād- (§188.III), to root in Skt. rādh- "effect, complete" ... DB 4.54; DNb 9, 10f; also in avahyarādiy'; the compound avahya-rādiy 'for this reason' is a stock formula of Darius' Bisotun inscription (DB 1.6f, 51; 4.47, 62). Pokorny files it in the dh-extension of *ar-: 'apers. rādiy (Lok. Sg.) "wegen"' under *rē-dh-, *rō-dh-, *rə-dh- alongside Skt. rādhnóti, Av. rādaiti 'macht bereit', NP ārāstan. Nourai's box, gloss and language label are all correct; the one live scholarly question is whether *reh₁dʰ-/*Hreh₁dʰ- is really an extension of *h₂er- (Pokorny, Walde-Pokorny, Watkins 1975) or an independent root (LIV, Etymonline, current AHD), and Kent himself pointedly separates it from '²rad-, pIE *rej-'.

nodes.derivation: Old Persian rādiy > Middle Persian rāδ/rāy ⟨l'd⟩, spelled ⟨rʾdy⟩ in inscriptional Middle Persian and Psalter Pahlavi and rendered r'd in Parthian, > New Persian را rā. The final -d, already a fricative δ in Middle Persian, is lost in New Persian, exactly as in MP pāδ > NP pā(y). Nyberg's glossary p. 164 is the key witness: '²rād [lʾd; inscr. and Ps. rʾdy] postpos. 1. for the sake of, because of, for ... 2. used as in NP: a) "to, for" ... b) denoting the dir. obj. of the pres. tense ... — OP rād- "reason, cause" in rādiy postpos. "on account of", avahya-rādiy "for this reason"; MPrth rʾd, MPrs rʾy; Paz. NP rā'. Horn no. 600 (p. 134) says the same: 'rā, zur Bezeichnung des Objekts dienende Partikel, rā "wegen" ... ap. rād- in -rādiy "wegen"; phlv. rāδ, rāi'; he adds that the object-marking use grows out of the original 'for, on account of, as regards'. چرا čerā 'why?' is the transparent compound če 'what' + rā 'for the sake of' = 'for what?', a Middle Persian formation (Nyberg: 'čē rād ... why? 35¹¹, 79⁵'); Wiktionary analyses it as چه (če) + رای (rā) 'reason'. Nourai's glosses are exact.

(a) ἁρμός harmós 'joint, fastening' < *h₂er-smo-, and its derivatives ἁρμόζω 'fit together', ἁρμονία 'joining, concord' — Pokorny 58-59 'gr. ἁρμός "Fuge, Zusammenfügung, Gelenk" ... ἁρμονία "Verbindung, Bund, Ebenmaß, Einklang"'; Watkins 'Suffixed form *arə-smo- in Greek harmos, joint, shoulder: HARMONY'. (b) ἄρθρον árthron 'joint' < *h₂er-dhro- + the Greek disease-suffix -ῖτις, hence ἀρθρῖτις 'arthritis' — Watkins 'Suffixed form *arə-dhro- in Greek arthron, joint: ARTHRO-'. (c) ἀριθμός arithmós 'number' — Watkins does place it here ('Variant (or separate root) *rī-. 2. Suffixed form *(ə)rī-dhmo- in Greek arithmos: ARITHMETIC, LOGARITHM') and Pokorny 61 lists it under the (ə)rī-, rei- base of ar-, but Klein derives it 'fr. I.-E. base *rī-, "to count, number"' and Etymonline from '*erei-dhmo-, suffixed variant form of root *re- "to reason, count"' — i.e. a base most current authorities keep separate from *h₂er-. (d) 'logos-arithmus' is not a Greek word at all: logarithmus is John Napier's Neo-Latin coinage of 1614 (Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio) from λόγος 'ratio' + ἀριθμός 'number'; putting it in a Greek box is an anachronism. (e) ἅρμα hárma is a real Greek word, but it means 'chariot, war-car' (Pokorny 59: 'gr. ἅρμα "Wagen"'), not 'arms, weapons'; 'arms, weapons' is Latin arma, -ōrum, which Pokorny lists on the same page and which Watkins files under I.1.b. Nourai has given the Greek word the Latin word's meaning — and it is that mistake that lets him hang the Arabic 'chariot' branch and English arms/army/alarm off this box.

nodes.derivation: All three are the ordinary learned French continuations. harmonie: Old French harmonie / armonie (12th c.), a Latinism taken from Latin harmonia, itself the Greek loan ἁρμονία; Klein: 'harmony, n. — ME. harmonie, fr. F. harmonie, fr. L. harmonia, fr. Gk. ἁρμονία'. arthrose: a 19th-20th c. French medical neologism (osteo-arthrose), Greek ἄρθρον 'joint' + the pathology suffix -ose (Greek -ωσις) used in French for non-inflammatory degenerative conditions, deliberately opposed to arthrite (-ῖτις, inflammatory). logarithme: French adaptation of Napier's Neo-Latin logarithmus (1614), current in French from the 1620s. Only the middle and last of these three actually pass through Greek as words; arthrose and logarithme are modern European coinages made out of Greek material.

nodes.derivation: The Arabic word intended is عَرَبَة ʿaraba(t), pl. ʿarabāt, 'cart, wagon' (Nourai's 'arbah, arobeh' transliterates it, and its Persianised عربه, without marking the initial ʿayn). It cannot come from Greek ἅρμα: a Greek initial h-/spiritus asper is never rendered by Arabic ʿayn, and the Greek stem is harm-, not ʿ-r-b. Modern references route the word the other way and outside Greek altogether. Lokotsch's Etymologisches Wörterbuch der europäischen Wörter orientalischen Ursprungs no. 90 files it as Turkish: 'Tk. araba: [Mit falscher arabisierender Schreibung ʿaraba] "Wagen", arabagï "Kutscher, Fuhrmann"' — i.e. the Arabic spelling with ʿayn is a false Arabicising orthography of a Turkish word (whence also Romanian araba, Russian arba, Serbian araba). Wiktionary's Turkish araba: 'Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عربه (araba). Ultimate origin uncertain', with Arabic عَرَبَة listed among the borrowings out of Turkic. Asbaghi's Persische Lehnwörter im Arabischen treats ʿarāba as a Persian loan in Arabic ('ʿarāba: "Wagen" pers., die arabisierte Form heißt عربه araba u. ʿarabāna, davon russ. serb. arab "Wagen"') and reports the Bahār-e ʿAjam view that the real word behind it is ʿarrāda 'Geschützlafette, Wurfgeschoßrad'. Vámbéry's Turco-Tatar dictionary already has Chagatai adak araba 'Gehwagen, Rollwagen'. No source consulted connects it to *h₂er-.

nodes.derivation: The Persian word is real: ارابه arrābe / ārābe 'cart, wagon, war-chariot', in Borhan-e Qate' (p. 96) 'ارابه - بر وزن فرابه، گردون را گویند' and in Mo'in '(اَ رّ بِ) (اِ.) گاری با دو چرخ که از چوب می‌ساختند و برای حمل بار از آن [استفاده می‌کردند]'. Nourai's parenthetical عرّاده is the rival spelling Dehkhoda records (Arabic ʿarrāda 'mangonel, siege engine, gun-carriage'), and Mo'in's اراده entry likewise cross-refers 'قس. عراده'. What is wrong is the route. Wiktionary derives Persian ارابه straight from Turkic: 'Borrowed from Turkic, from the same source as Turkish araba' (with the Tajik doublet ароба). Asbaghi runs it the opposite way, Persian → Arabic ʿarāba, and offers as the older Iranian comparison Av. raθa- / OP *rāda 'chariot' — a word of PIE *Hroth₂o- 'wheel' from the root *Hret- 'to run', which has nothing to do with *h₂er- 'to fit together'. Neither Borhan-e Qate' nor Mo'in nor Dehkhoda gives any Greek or Arabic origin tag. Greek ἅρμα → Arabic ʿaraba → Persian arrābe is therefore an etymology unique to Nourai, and it is phonetically impossible on the Arabic side (see node 11).

nodes.words: harmony, arthritis, arithmetic, logarithm, arms, army, alarm
nodes.derivation: All seven words are listed by Watkins under ar-, so the root attribution is his; but the chart's arrow, which makes them all descend from the Greek box, is right for only four of them. harmony (late 14c.) ← Old French harmonie ← Latin harmonia ← Greek ἁρμονία; arthritis (1540s) ← Latin arthritis ← Greek ἀρθρῖτις; arithmetic (mid-13c. arsmetike) ← Old French arismetique ← Latin arithmetica ← Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη); logarithm (1610s) ← Napier's Neo-Latin logarithmus. But arms (early 14c.) and army (late 14c.) come from Latin arma through French — Klein: 'army, n. — F. armée, fr. L. armata, fem. pp. of armare, "to furnish with weapons"'; Etymonline: 'Latin arma "tools, arms" ... PIE *ar(ə)mo-, suffixed form of root *ar- "to fit together"' — and alarm (late 14c.) is Old French alarme from Italian all'arme! 'to (the) arms!', again Latin arma. None of the last three touches Greek. Note also that Etymonline and Klein trace arithmetic to a base *re-/*rī- 'to reason, count' rather than to *ar- proper.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر هفت واژه در پیوست واتکینز ذیل همین ریشه آمده‌اند، پس نسبت‌دادن آنها به ریشه از آنِ اوست؛ اما پیکان نمودار که همه را از جعبهٔ یونانی می‌آویزد تنها دربارهٔ چهار واژه درست است. harmony از فرانسوی کهن و لاتینی و در نهایت ἁρμονία یونانی؛ arthritis از ἀρθρῖτις یونانی از راه لاتینی؛ arithmetic از فرانسوی کهن arismetique و لاتینی arithmetica از یونانی؛ و logarithm از logarithmus لاتینی نو. ولی arms و army از arma لاتینی از راه فرانسه آمده‌اند (کلاین: army از armée فرانسوی، از armata لاتینی) و alarm از all'arme ایتالیایی «به سلاح!» است که آن هم به arma لاتینی برمی‌گردد؛ هیچ‌یک از این سه به یونانی نمی‌رسد. افزون بر این، کلاین و اتیمانلاین ریشهٔ arithmetic را پایهٔ جداگانهٔ *rī-/*rē- «شمردن» می‌دانند. پس این گره با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Two of the three are secure, the third is contested. (a) ars, gen. artis 'skill, craft' is *h₂er-ti-, formally the exact match of Skt. r̥tí- 'manner' and Middle High German art; Pokorny 58: 'lat. ars, -tis "die Geschicklichkeit, Kunst, Art und Weise" (eigentlich "Zusammenfügung, Gabe richtig zusammenzufügen" = mhd. art)'; Watkins '*arə-ti- in Latin ars (stem art-), art, skill, craft'. (b) reor, rērī 'to reckon, think', p.p. ratus, whence ratiō 'reckoning, reason' — Pokorny 59 puts them under the variant *rē-, rō-, with the nice observation that 'das primitivste Zählen wird vom Aufeinanderlegen oder -schichten der zu zählenden Stücke begleitet'. (c) ōrdō, -inis 'row, order', with ōrdior 'to begin to weave' — Nourai's gloss 'row of threads in loom' is Watkins' own wording ('Latin ōrdō, order (originally a row of threads in a loom)'), but Watkins prefixes it 'Possibly suffixed variant form (or separate root) *ōr-dh-', Pokorny 61 introduces the whole group with 'Trifft der Zusammenhang mit ar- "fügen" ... zu' (i.e. 'if the connection holds'), and Etymonline calls the *ar- origin 'uncertain', preferring Proto-Italic *ordn- 'row, order'. Hence the node as a whole is plausible rather than confirmed.

nodes.derivation: آرتیست ārtist is a direct 20th-century borrowing of French artiste, taken over with the imported theatre and cinema (the word is at home in Persian from the 1300s Sh./1920s-30s onward, and in colloquial Persian it has developed the extra sense 'poseur, one who plays a part to get his way'). The French final -e is not represented in Persian; the initial ā- is written آ; the -is- of artiste is kept as ـیس, which shows the loan came through the French spelling/pronunciation rather than through English artist (which would have given *ârtist with a different vowel value in the second syllable). Mo'in tags the word '[فر.]', his own mark for a French loan: '[فر.] (ص.) هنرمند، هنرپیشه؛ کنایه از: آدمی که برای رسیدن به خواسته‌هایش نقش بازی کند'.

nodes.words: order, coordinate, ordinary, reason, ratio, rate
nodes.derivation: All six are Latinate and all six come from the two Latin stems in the parent box. From ōrdō, ōrdinis: order (c. 1200) ← Old French ordre ← Latin ōrdinem; ordinary (early 15c.) ← Latin ōrdinārius 'of the usual order'; coordinate (1640s) ← Medieval Latin coordinare 'to set in the same order' (co- + ōrdinare). From reor, ratus: reason (c. 1200) ← Old French raison ← Latin ratiōnem; ratio (1630s) is the Latin word taken over unchanged in its mathematical sense; rate (early 15c.) ← Old French rate ← Medieval Latin rata (pars) 'reckoned (part)', from ratus, the past participle of rērī. Watkins lists exactly this set: 'ORDAIN, ORDER, ORDINAL, ORDINANCE, ORDINARY, ORDINATE, ORDO; COORDINATION, INORDINATE, SUBORDINATE' and 'RATE¹, RATIO, REASON; (ARRAIGN)'. (Whether ōrdō itself belongs to *h₂er- is the open question flagged at node 14; the Latin→English step charted here is not in doubt.)
nodes.derivation_fa: هر شش واژه لاتینی‌تبارند و از همان دو ستاک جعبهٔ بالادست می‌آیند. از ōrdō/ōrdinis: order (حدود ۱۲۰۰ میلادی) از ordre فرانسوی کهن و ōrdinem لاتینی؛ ordinary (اوایل سدهٔ پانزدهم) از ōrdinārius لاتینی؛ coordinate (دههٔ ۱۶۴۰) از coordinare لاتینی میانه «در یک رده نهادن». از reor/ratus: reason (حدود ۱۲۰۰) از raison فرانسوی کهن و ratiōnem لاتینی؛ ratio (دههٔ ۱۶۳۰) خودِ واژهٔ لاتینی است که در معنی ریاضی وام گرفته شده؛ و rate (اوایل سدهٔ پانزدهم) از rata (pars) لاتینی میانه «بخشِ شمرده‌شده» از اسم مفعول ratus. واتکینز دقیقاً همین مجموعه را برمی‌شمارد. تنها پرسش باز، همان تردید دربارهٔ تعلق ōrdō به ریشهٔ *h₂er- است که در گرهٔ ۱۴ گفته شد؛ گذر از لاتینی به انگلیسی در اینجا تردیدی ندارد و ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: An unlabelled pass-through box for the two Germanic stems Watkins derives from this root: Proto-Germanic *armaz 'arm' (< PIE *h₂erH-mo- 'joint, upper arm', the exact match of Skt. īrmá-, Av. arəma-, Latin armus, Old Prussian irmo, OCS ramo) and Proto-Germanic *rēdaną 'to advise' (< the *rē-dh- variant), whence OHG rātan, Gothic garēdan, Old Norse ráða, Old English rǣdan. Pokorny 59 sets out the first ('B. Von der schweren Basis arə-mo-: r̥-mo- "Arm". Ai. īrmá-ḥ "Arm, Vorderbug" = av. arəma- "Arm" ... got. arms, ahd. usw. arm "Arm"') and p. 60 the second ('ahd. rātan "raten, beratschlagen" ... as. rādan, anord. ráda, ags. rǣdan (letzteres auch "lesen", engl. read)').
nodes.derivation_fa: این جعبهٔ بی‌واژه نمایندهٔ دو ستاک ژرمنی است که واتکینز از این ریشه می‌گیرد: ژرمنی آغازین *armaz «بازو» از *h₂erH-mo- «مفصل، بازو» که همتای دقیق īrmá- سنسکریت، arəma- اوستایی، armus لاتینی و ramo اسلاوی کهن است؛ و ژرمنی آغازین *rēdaną «اندرز دادن» از گونهٔ *rē-dh-، که rātan آلمانی علیای کهن، garēdan گوتی، ráða نورس کهن و rǣdan انگلیسی کهن از آن است. پوکورنی در صفحهٔ ۵۹ دستهٔ نخست و در صفحهٔ ۶۰ دستهٔ دوم را می‌آورد و در همان‌جا می‌نویسد rǣdan انگلیسی کهن «خواندن» هم معنی می‌دهد (read امروزی). ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: arm (the limb) is beyond doubt: Old English earm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz, from PIE *h₂erH-mo- 'joint, upper arm'; Klein 'arm, n., the upper limb. — ME., fr. OE. earm, arm, rel. to OS., Dan., Swed., MDu., Du., MHG., G. arm, ON. armr, ... Goth. arms, "arm", and cogn. with OI. īrmáḥ, Avestic arəma-, "arm", Arm. armukn, "elbow", Osset. arm, "palm of the hand", Gk. ἁρμός, "a joint", L. armus, "shoulder"'; Buck (Selected Synonyms 4.30) lists the same set under '*ar(ə)-'. read is the doubtful half: Old English rǣdan 'to advise, counsel, interpret, guess', Proto-Germanic *rēdaną, and the specialisation to 'interpret written signs' is a shared English-Norse innovation (OE rǣdan, ON ráða) alongside the noun rǣd 'counsel'. Watkins (1975/1985) does file it here, under 'Variant or separate root *rē- (< *reə-) ... Suffixed form *rē-dh-'; but the hedge in that heading is real: Etymonline gives read a root of its own, '*re- "to reason, count"', and current reconstructions posit *Hreh₁dʰ- 'to succeed, accomplish' independent of *h₂er-. So the arm arrow is confirmed and the read arrow is only plausible.
nodes.derivation_fa: «arm» انگلیسی به معنی بازو تردیدناپذیر است: از earm انگلیسی کهن، از *armaz ژرمنی آغازین، از *h₂erH-mo- «مفصل، بازو»؛ کلاین آن را با īrmá- سنسکریت، arəma- اوستایی، armukn ارمنی «آرنج»، arm آسی «کف دست»، ἁρμός یونانی و armus لاتینی هم‌ریشه می‌داند و باک نیز همین گروه را ذیل *ar(ə)- می‌آورد. اما «read» نیمهٔ مشکوک این گره است: از rǣdan انگلیسی کهن «اندرز دادن، تفسیر کردن، حدس زدن» و *rēdaną ژرمنی آغازین؛ تخصیص معنایی آن به «خواندنِ نوشته» نوآوریِ مشترک انگلیسی و نورس است. واتکینز آن را ذیل همین ریشه ولی با قید «گونه یا ریشهٔ جداگانهٔ *rē-» آورده؛ اتیمانلاین ریشهٔ آن را جداگانه *re- «شمردن، اندیشیدن» می‌داند و بازسازی‌های امروزی *Hreh₁dʰ- را مستقل از *h₂er- می‌گیرند. پس پیکانِ arm درست و پیکانِ read با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.
